analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a single 19% flat tax on wages and business income.
analysis.headline: The flat-tax bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap the current income tax and replace it with one flat rate of 19%, dropping to 17% after 2007, applied to wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits. It would repeal the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, and every income tax credit — including the child tax credit and the earned income credit. Investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest would no longer be taxed for individuals, and corporations would pay a flat tax on business income instead.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and wealthy families gain the most: the top rate falls from 35% to 19%, capital gains, dividends, and interest would not be taxed at all at the individual level, the estate and gift taxes would be repealed outright, and the alternative minimum tax would disappear [S2][S3]. Employers also gain, because pension nondiscrimination rules and limits on contributions would be repealed and employers could pull excess assets out of pension plans with only income tax owed [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, wealthy estates, and employers

how_it_helps.text: It caps all individual tax rates at 19%, falling to 17% after 2007, replacing the current system that taxed top income at 35% [S2][S3].

Taxable income would consist only of wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, so income from capital gains, dividends, and interest would no longer be taxed at the individual level [S2][S3].
It repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after 2005 [S2][S3].
It repeals the alternative minimum tax and all income tax credits [S2][S3].
It repeals pension nondiscrimination rules, contribution limits, and distribution restrictions, and lets employers reclaim excess pension assets by paying income tax on the amount [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Middle-income working families would bear the cost: they would lose the child tax credit, the earned income credit, and deductions for mortgage interest, charitable giving, and state and local taxes, while their wages remain fully taxed. A family of four earning around $50,000 in wages would owe tax under the flat rate that it largely does not owe today. Workers could also be affected if employers respond to the new rules on pension plans and fringe benefits by scaling back benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-income wage earners who lose tax credits

drawbacks.text: It repeals all income tax credits, eliminating the child tax credit and the earned income credit that reduce or erase tax bills for low- and middle-income working families [S2][S3].
It ends deductions for mortgage interest, charitable giving, and state and local taxes, which are used heavily by middle-income homeowners [S2].

It repeals pension nondiscrimination rules that prevent plans from favoring executives over rank-and-file workers, removes limits on contributions and distributions, and allows employers to reclaim excess pension assets — changes that shift risk onto workers' retirement security [S2][S3].

It writes a rule requiring a three-fifths supermajority of both chambers to raise any income tax rate, cut the standard deduction, or restore any tax benefit, making future tax policy changes far harder to enact [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Simplification is a real benefit — a flat tax on wages and business income with a large standard deduction would be far easier to file. But the distributional cost is severe: the bill untaxes investment income entirely for individuals, repeals the estate tax, and eliminates every credit and deduction that currently shelters working and middle-class families, so the tax burden would shift toward wage earners while wealth holders' taxes fall sharply. The pension deregulation and supermajority lock-in add longer-term risks on top of that.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day, sat there for the rest of the 109th Congress with no hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the Tax Simplification Act of 2005 on May 23, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
Two Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Middle- and low-income taxpayers are better off because the bill died: their credits, deductions, and pension protections stayed intact. Wealthy households and employers lost the chance at estate tax repeal, untaxed investment income, and pension asset reversions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families whose credits and pensions were spared

sides.party_line_note: All three senators attached to the bill — the sponsor and both cosponsors — were Republicans, and there is no Democratic support anywhere in the record; no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The top rate drops from 35% to 19%, capital gains, dividends, and interest go untaxed for individuals, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes are repealed. The revenue foregone would otherwise be part of the base that funds government; under this bill the shift in burden falls on wages.

Pension nondiscrimination rules, contribution limits, and distribution restrictions are repealed, and employers can reclaim excess pension assets by paying income tax on the amount — freeing employer funds at the expense of worker retirement protections.

These employers would owe a 19% tax on the value of noncash employee benefits like health coverage, a cost that would be borne by students, patients, and taxpayers through higher prices or reduced services.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A flat tax with a single rate and a standard deduction would sharply reduce demand for paid tax preparation and compliance services, while filers benefit from simpler filing.
